title: MedOrbit Health x Redwood Inference — Security review (SOC 2, retention, audit logs)
summary: MedOrbit reviewed Redwood’s security posture for a PHI-adjacent workload, focusing on SOC 2 evidence, data retention defaults, audit logging/export, and residency controls. Redwood clarified Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment boundaries, encryption/KMS options, and what is configurable today vs requires an exception. MedOrbit requested specific evidence (SOC 2 Type II, pen test summary, subprocessor list, DPA/BAA posture, audit log samples) and proposed a follow-up technical session on SIEM export and VPC networking.
topics: SOC 2 Type II scope and evidence sharing under NDA
HIPAA / PHI handling assumptions and BAA/DPA questions
Audit logging: what events are logged, retention, export to SIEM
Encryption in transit/at rest, KMS and HSM integration points
Data residency / region pinning for regulated workloads
SSO/SAML, RBAC, least-privilege access and support access
Incident response, DR/BCP basics and customer responsibilities in Private
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC 2 Type II report and bridge letter under NDA (or confirm NDA status).
Redwood to send security packet: subprocessor list, incident response overview, DR/BCP summary, and SSO/RBAC documentation.
Redwood to provide written answers on prompt/output retention defaults for Hosted/Dedicated and expectations for Private/VPC deployments.
Redwood to share an example audit log schema + supported export options (format/destination) and retention controls.
Schedule 45-min technical follow-up with MedOrbit platform team on SIEM export + VPC networking assumptions.
MedOrbit to confirm target region/residency requirements and whether on-prem is a hard requirement or a phase-2.
action_items: Olga Petrov: Confirm NDA status with MedOrbit; if active, deliver SOC 2 Type II report + bridge letter by 2026-01-20.
Marcus Lin: Provide pen test executive summary and vulnerability management overview by 2026-01-22.
Dr. Aisha Rahman: Send incident response and access-to-production policy summary (support access controls) by 2026-01-21.
Markus Klein: Share audit log sample schema + SIEM export notes (Splunk/HTTP/S3 patterns) by 2026-01-21.
Avery Johnson: Coordinate follow-up technical session times; propose 2 slots by 2026-01-19.
MedOrbit (Priya Nair): Send MedOrbit’s questionnaire section on retention/residency and PHI scope assumptions by 2026-01-20.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: MedOrbit Health x Redwood Inference — Security review (SOC 2, retention, audit logs)
Date: Jan 16, 2026 3:03 PM ET
Duration: 53 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering), Dr. Aisha Rahman (CISO), Olga Petrov (GRC), Marcus Lin (Security Eng)
MedOrbit Health: Tanya Brooks (Security & Risk), Eli Chen (IT / Cloud Security), Priya Nair (GRC), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Laura Gomez (Privacy Counsel)

— — —

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. Folks can hear me okay?

[00:02] Tanya Brooks: Yep.

[00:03] Markus Klein: Yep, loud and clear.

[00:05] Avery Johnson: Great. Thanks everyone for making the time. This is the security review follow-up from last week’s product overview. Goal today is to walk through your top concerns—SOC 2, retention, audit logging, and residency—and leave with a list of evidence we can share and the next steps. Aisha and Olga are here from our side, plus Marcus from security engineering. 

[00:23] Priya Nair: Perfect. I’m going to be a bit process-y, sorry in advance. 

[00:26] Dr. Aisha Rahman: That’s our favorite kind of meeting.

[00:28] (crosstalk)

[00:30] Avery Johnson: Tanya, do you want to kick with what you need to get comfortable to move to a pilot?

[00:35] Tanya Brooks: Yep. So we’re evaluating you for a… I’ll call it “PHI adjacent” product feature, but it could very quickly become in-scope. We’ve had issues with vendors who say they don’t store anything and then later there’s logs everywhere. So we need very direct answers on: do you store prompts and outputs, for how long, can we turn it off, and what audit logs we can export to our SIEM. And then SOC 2, pen test, and a subprocessor list. Basic stuff.

[01:05] Avery Johnson: Totally. Markus, do you want to frame deployment modes first, because some of the answers differ between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.

[01:13] Markus Klein: Yeah. Quick framing: Redwood has three main modes. Hosted API is our multi-tenant managed service. Dedicated is single-tenant reserved capacity in our cloud account, still managed by us but isolated. Private is deployed into your environment—typically your VPC—with customer-managed networking boundaries. For Private, the data plane is inside your boundary, and the control plane interactions are limited and documented. So when we talk retention and logs, it’s important which of those you’re evaluating.

[01:43] Samir Patel: For us, we’re leaning Private in our AWS VPC, maybe with VPC peering. But we also want to understand if Dedicated is enough for phase one. 

[01:53] Tanya Brooks: Yeah, Dedicated might be acceptable if retention is “no store” and audit logs are strong.

[02:01] Olga Petrov: Understood. We can be precise there, but I’m going to caveat we’ll use “configurable” vs “default” language.

[02:08] Priya Nair: Great. First question: SOC 2. Do you have Type II, what period, what scope, and can we see it without NDA?

[02:17] Olga Petrov: We have SOC 2 Type II. Current report period is the last 12 months—covers Security, Availability, and Confidentiality. We share the full report under NDA. Without NDA we can share a short attestation letter and a security overview, but not the detailed controls and testing results.

[02:36] Laura Gomez: Is HIPAA in scope of SOC 2? I know that’s not exactly how SOC works, but—

[02:41] Olga Petrov: Right, SOC 2 isn’t “HIPAA certification.” What we can do is map relevant controls to HIPAA Security Rule requirements. We also have a standard DPA. For BAA—Aisha can speak—depending on deployment mode we have a posture, but we typically handle BAA discussions as part of the enterprise terms.

[03:00] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yeah. HIPAA: we do sign BAAs for certain customers, generally when deployment mode and data handling align. In practice, teams doing Private in their VPC find it cleaner because PHI doesn’t traverse our multi-tenant environment. But we should treat this as: you define whether you are sending PHI; we design the architecture so you can keep it in your boundary if needed.

[03:24] Tanya Brooks: Okay. So if we did Hosted, you’re saying you might see PHI.

[03:28] Markus Klein: If you send PHI to Hosted, then yes, it’s transiting and processed in our environment. We encrypt in transit and at rest, access is controlled, but it’s still in our boundary. With Private, the inference cluster sits in your VPC, and you can keep network egress locked down.

[03:46] Eli Chen: When you say “control plane,” does Redwood still have access into the cluster?

[03:51] Marcus Lin: We design it so we don’t need interactive shell access as a default. Support access is gated, time-bound, and logged, and can be disabled or require your approval depending on configuration. For Private, we typically rely on customer-provided telemetry and you can choose what gets exported.

[04:10] Priya Nair: That’s a little hand-wavy. Is there a document that spells out operational responsibility and what “support access” means?

[04:17] Markus Klein: Yes—responsibility matrix and reference architecture. We can share a Private/VPC architecture doc that includes who owns patching, monitoring, networking, and what remote access patterns exist.

[04:31] Tanya Brooks: Put that on the evidence list.

[04:34] Avery Johnson: Will do.

[04:36] Priya Nair: Next: retention. Do you store prompts and outputs? I need it per deployment type.

[04:44] Olga Petrov: For Hosted and Dedicated: by default we retain certain request metadata for operational purposes—like timestamps, model, token counts, error codes. Prompt and output content retention is configurable; we have options to minimize or disable content logging. We do not use customer prompts/outputs to train our models.

[05:06] Tanya Brooks: “Configurable” meaning what exactly? Like a checkbox in console, or an email to support?

[05:12] Markus Klein: Today it’s an account-level setting we configure with you, and we document it. In the console you’ll still see usage metrics, but content can be redacted/not stored.

[05:23] Samir Patel: When you say “not stored,” is that “not written to disk” or “written but short TTL”?

[05:29] Marcus Lin: Good question. For the hosted service, requests are processed in-memory and then—depending on your logging settings—some data may be written to our logging systems. With content logging disabled, the prompt and output bodies are not persisted in our application logs. There is still transient processing and standard infrastructure logs, but we avoid persisting the payload.

[05:54] Laura Gomez: What about exceptions? Like error traces, debugging dumps, that kind of thing.

[05:59] Marcus Lin: We have policies that restrict that. If there’s an incident and we need payload-level troubleshooting, we would request explicit approval, and we can do that via a secure capture mechanism. But default behavior is: content is not retained when configured.

[06:14] Tanya Brooks: I’ll be honest, we’ve heard that before. We need it in writing, with exact categories: application logs, access logs, audit logs, support tickets, etc.

[06:24] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Completely fair. We can provide a written “data handling and retention” statement for your security questionnaire, broken down by categories. We’ll keep it aligned to what we actually do today.

[06:36] Priya Nair: What’s the retention period for the metadata you mentioned?

[06:40] Olga Petrov: Standard operational metadata retention is on the order of weeks to a couple months depending on system; we can provide the exact ranges in the questionnaire response. For enterprise agreements we can align retention windows and exports.

[06:56] Eli Chen: And Private?

[06:58] Markus Klein: For Private, since it’s in your VPC, you control logging and retention. Our software emits logs; you decide where they go—CloudWatch, Splunk forwarder, S3, whatever—and you own the retention policy. We can recommend defaults.

[07:15] Samir Patel: That’s more like it.

[07:18] Tanya Brooks: Okay. Audit logging. What do you log? And can we export it?

[07:24] Marcus Lin: We have audit logs for control-plane actions: user authentication events, SSO logins, API key creation/rotation, RBAC changes, model deployment changes (like pinning a model version), and admin actions in the console. For request-level logs, we have request metadata logs, but not necessarily full payload content—again depends on your settings.

[07:48] Priya Nair: Can those audit logs be exported automatically to our SIEM?

[07:53] Markus Klein: Yes. In Hosted and Dedicated, we can support export mechanisms—typically secure delivery to your S3 bucket or an HTTPS endpoint, depending on your SIEM pipeline. In Private, it’s native because logs are already in your account.

[08:10] Eli Chen: Format? JSON? CEF?

[08:13] Marcus Lin: JSON is the common. We can provide a schema sample. If you require CEF, we usually do that via a transformer in your pipeline rather than emitting CEF directly.

[08:27] Tanya Brooks: And retention of audit logs on your side, for Hosted.

[08:31] Olga Petrov: We retain audit logs per our standard policy; for enterprise customers we can negotiate and/or provide export so you can store them longer in your system.

[08:43] Tanya Brooks: We typically need 1 year minimum in SIEM.

[08:46] Markus Klein: Understood. That’s why export is important. We’ll confirm the out-of-the-box retention and how export can meet your one-year requirement.

[08:57] Laura Gomez: Residency. Where is the data processed? Can we pin to US only? We have some patients in EU too, but the initial product is US.

[09:08] Markus Klein: For Hosted/Dedicated, you can select region(s) and keep processing in that region. For Private, it runs wherever you deploy it—in your VPC, in your chosen region. 

[09:20] Priya Nair: Do you have any subcontractors that would move data cross-border? Like support teams outside US, or logging vendors.

[09:29] Olga Petrov: We do use subprocessors for infrastructure and some operational tooling. We maintain a subprocessor list and we can share it. Access to customer environments is role-based; support access is controlled. We can also restrict support to certain geographies for some enterprise arrangements—again, it depends on contract.

[09:52] Tanya Brooks: Put it on the list. Subprocessors and where they are located.

[09:56] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[10:00] Samir Patel: Switching to encryption and key management: do you support customer-managed keys? Like KMS? Or HSM.

[10:07] Marcus Lin: For Hosted/Dedicated, encryption at rest uses cloud provider encryption. We have KMS-backed encryption and can discuss customer-managed key options for certain tiers. For Private, you can use your own KMS keys in your account. For HSM, generally we integrate at the KMS/HSM boundary where your key material is managed by your provider—AWS CloudHSM, etc. We don’t usually integrate directly to bespoke on-prem HSM unless it’s part of your KMS layer.

[10:34] Eli Chen: So for Private in AWS, we can use our KMS CMKs. That’s fine.

[10:39] Tanya Brooks: Access controls. Do you have SSO? SAML? SCIM?

[10:44] Marcus Lin: SSO via SAML is supported. RBAC is supported for the console. SCIM—depends on the tier; we can confirm current status. We can also enforce MFA for local accounts, but most customers do SSO.

[11:04] Priya Nair: Can you provide a list of roles and permissions? We need it for least privilege review.

[11:09] Markus Klein: Yes, we have a role matrix. We’ll share that.

[11:14] Laura Gomez: On privacy: you said you don’t train on our data. Is that contractual?

[11:18] Avery Johnson: Yes, it’s in our terms. We can highlight that clause.

[11:22] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And it’s enforced by internal policy and technical controls. We don’t commingle customer payloads into any model training pipeline.

[11:34] Tanya Brooks: Incident response. If something happens, what’s the notification window?

[11:39] Olga Petrov: Our standard terms define notification timing, and for enterprise we can align to your requirements. We have an incident response plan, and it’s tested.

[11:49] Priya Nair: We’ll need the IR policy summary and last tabletop date.

[11:54] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We can share a summary and evidence of testing cadence, yes. Some details are restricted but we can provide enough for your vendor risk file.

[12:05] Samir Patel: Availability/DR? If Hosted goes down, what happens? For Private, do we run multi-AZ?

[12:12] Markus Klein: Hosted and Dedicated have defined SLAs depending on tier. For Private, you can design it multi-AZ in your VPC. We’ll provide reference patterns—active/active or active/passive depending on your latency tolerance.

[12:28] Tanya Brooks: Okay. I want to return to retention because that’s our big red flag area. Specifically: are prompts/outputs ever stored for “analytics” or “debugging” automatically.

[12:39] Marcus Lin: Not for analytics as in content analytics. We track token usage, latency metrics, error rates, those kinds of telemetry. If content logging is enabled, content may appear in logs for troubleshooting; if disabled, it should not. We can also provide guidance to avoid sending PHI in Hosted if you’re not comfortable.

[13:01] Laura Gomez: “Should not” isn’t good enough.

[13:03] Marcus Lin: Fair. I’m speaking conversationally. In writing, we’ll be definitive: when content logging is disabled, prompt/output bodies are not persisted in our standard logs. The remaining retained data is metadata. We’ll enumerate it.

[13:19] Priya Nair: Is there any caching? Like KV cache? I’ve heard that term. Does that mean you keep data around.

[13:26] Markus Klein: KV cache is an in-memory performance optimization for the model during generation. It’s not like a database cache. It’s ephemeral and tied to the request. We also have optional prefix caching for performance—again ephemeral and typically scoped, and in Private you control it entirely. In hosted modes, caching can be enabled to reduce cost/latency, but we can disable it if it conflicts with your policies.

[13:53] Eli Chen: Is that documented? 

[13:55] Markus Klein: We can provide a short technical note. The term gets scary because it’s “cache,” but it’s not retention in the compliance sense.

[14:07] Tanya Brooks: Good, but we’ll need it. 

[14:10] Avery Johnson: I’m capturing: retention categories in writing, and caching explanation.

[14:15] Priya Nair: On audit logs, do you log admin actions by Redwood employees?

[14:20] Marcus Lin: We log privileged access events and administrative actions in our systems. For Private deployments, if we have any support access, it’s logged and can be made visible to you. We can provide our policy around that and the type of records generated.

[14:39] Tanya Brooks: Are audit logs immutable?

[14:42] Marcus Lin: Within our systems, they are protected and access-controlled. For your SIEM, once exported into your storage with WORM controls, you can make them immutable as per your policy. If you require immutability guarantees, we can speak to how the pipeline is secured and signed.

[15:01] Samir Patel: Signed logs? Like tamper-evident.

[15:04] Marcus Lin: We don’t currently cryptographically sign each audit event payload as a product feature. We can talk about compensating controls—restricted write access, append-only storage in your environment, CloudTrail alignment, etc. 

[15:20] Tanya Brooks: Okay, that’s important. We might be okay with SIEM immutability. But let’s note: no per-event signing today.

[15:28] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Correct. And we’ll make sure that’s clearly stated.

[15:33] Priya Nair: Pen test: when was the last one, and can we see results.

[15:38] Olga Petrov: We do third-party penetration testing at least annually and also ongoing vulnerability scanning. We can share an executive summary and remediation attestation, under NDA.

[15:51] Tanya Brooks: Good.

[15:53] Laura Gomez: Subprocessors and DPA. We’ll need your DPA template. And if we move to a BAA, we’ll need that template too.

[16:01] Avery Johnson: Yep. We can share DPA template now. BAA template typically once we confirm deployment approach and scope, but we can start the conversation.

[16:12] Samir Patel: Also, network. If we do Private in our VPC, do we need outbound internet from the cluster?

[16:19] Markus Klein: Not necessarily. The Private package can be deployed with restricted egress. There may be optional egress for updates or telemetry, but we can support a “no outbound” posture with documented allowlists. That’s part of the architecture review.

[16:36] Eli Chen: We will require strict egress allowlist. We’ve been burned by “phone home” dependencies.

[16:42] Markus Klein: Understood. We can map out all required endpoints. And in some cases we can provide offline update artifacts, but let’s confirm your constraints.

[16:55] Priya Nair: Is Private GA or beta.

[16:58] Markus Klein: Private is in active production with enterprise customers. Some components may be newer depending on features (like certain export integrations), but the core deployment is mature.

[17:12] Tanya Brooks: Okay.

[17:14] Avery Johnson: Tanya, can I ask: is your main blocker “we need proof” or “we need Private only.”

[17:19] Tanya Brooks: Both. If you can meet “no payload retention” in Dedicated and give us the evidence fast, we can pilot. But long term we probably need Private because product leadership wants to move faster without constant vendor reviews.

[17:35] Laura Gomez: Also, if we do Dedicated in your environment, the legal stance is different. With Private we can argue it’s our system. Not fully, but… you know.

[17:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We see that pattern often.

[17:48] Priya Nair: Okay, let’s go down my questionnaire sections. I’ll ask rapid fire.

[17:54] Avery Johnson: Go for it.

[17:56] Priya Nair: Authentication: SSO, MFA.

[17:59] Marcus Lin: SAML SSO supported, MFA available, RBAC for roles.

[18:04] Priya Nair: Password policy.

[18:06] Marcus Lin: Strong password requirements for local accounts; but most customers use SSO.

[18:10] Priya Nair: Logging and monitoring.

[18:12] Marcus Lin: Centralized logging, monitoring, alerting. Audit logs as discussed.

[18:18] Priya Nair: Vulnerability management and patching.

[18:21] Marcus Lin: Continuous scanning, regular patch cycles, change management controls.

[18:26] Priya Nair: Data classification.

[18:28] Olga Petrov: We have internal data classification; customer data treated as confidential.

[18:32] Priya Nair: Backups.

[18:34] Markus Klein: Hosted/Dedicated have backup and DR processes; Private is customer-configurable, we provide guidance.

[18:42] Priya Nair: Subprocessors.

[18:44] Olga Petrov: Yes, list available.

[18:47] Priya Nair: Where are support staff located.

[18:50] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Primarily North America and Europe. Access is controlled and logged. We can discuss geo restrictions as a requirement.

[18:59] Tanya Brooks: Okay. Now about PHI: will you sign BAA for Hosted.

[19:04] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Potentially, but we would need to scope it. Generally we prefer Private for PHI because it limits exposure and reduces complexity. But it’s not an automatic “no.”

[19:16] Laura Gomez: Understood.

[19:18] Eli Chen: One thing: do you integrate with CloudTrail in Private? Like, can we see actions as CloudTrail events.

[19:24] Markus Klein: In Private, many actions are in your AWS account so you can use native AWS logging for infrastructure actions. Application-level audit events are emitted as logs; those can be shipped into CloudWatch and then your SIEM.

[19:40] Eli Chen: Okay.

[19:42] Tanya Brooks: I want to ask about model providers. Are you calling out to third-party model APIs?

[19:48] Markus Klein: No, in our platform the models run on our inference runtime on GPU infrastructure. We’re not proxying to, like, Anthropic or Azure OpenAI. In Private, the model artifacts are deployed into your environment.

[20:04] Samir Patel: So no external API calls at inference time.

[20:07] Markus Klein: Correct, unless you configure something custom. Default: no.

[20:12] Tanya Brooks: Good.

[20:14] Priya Nair: Data deletion. If we terminate, do you delete our data.

[20:18] Olga Petrov: Yes. There’s a process for deletion of customer data as defined in the DPA, subject to legal retention requirements. For Private, you own the environment so deletion is in your control.

[20:33] Laura Gomez: Do you have a standard data retention schedule that references those legal holds.

[20:38] Olga Petrov: Yes, we can summarize it.

[20:41] Tanya Brooks: Access reviews. Do you do periodic access reviews.

[20:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes. Regular access reviews, least privilege principles, and separation of duties.

[20:52] Priya Nair: Ok. Can we talk about audit logs specifically for API usage? We need to know who called what.

[21:00] Markus Klein: If you use API keys, usage is tied to key identity. With SSO-based user access in console, you can also attribute admin actions. For request logs, you can include your own request IDs and metadata for correlation. We can help standardize that.

[21:18] Samir Patel: So if our application uses one API key, we won’t get per-human attribution.

[21:22] Markus Klein: Right, unless you segment keys by service or tenant. Many customers create per-service keys and rotate.

[21:30] Tanya Brooks: We’ll do that.

[21:33] Eli Chen: Another thing: do you support private connectivity—PrivateLink, VPC peering.

[21:39] Markus Klein: For Dedicated/Hosted there are options for private connectivity depending on region and tier; for Private, it’s in your VPC so you can do peering, PrivateLink, transit gateway, etc.

[21:53] Avery Johnson: We should probably schedule a technical follow-up for the connectivity and SIEM export details.

[21:58] Samir Patel: Yes, with my team.

[22:01] Tanya Brooks: Back to evidence. Here’s what we need this week if possible: SOC 2 Type II, pen test summary, subprocessor list, IR policy summary, and written retention statement. Also, a sample audit log event.

[22:16] Avery Johnson: That’s doable. NDA might gate SOC 2 and pen test, but we can move fast if NDA is in place.

[22:23] Laura Gomez: We have an NDA executed with you from procurement, I think. But I’m not 100% sure it covers this entity.

[22:30] Avery Johnson: Olga, can you confirm on your side.

[22:33] Olga Petrov: Yes, I’ll check after the call and confirm by email. Worst case, we send an NDA link for signature same day.

[22:41] Priya Nair: Great.

[22:43] Tanya Brooks: And just to be clear, we need the retention answer to include: how long you keep request metadata, and whether you keep IP addresses.

[22:51] Marcus Lin: We do log IPs for security purposes in some contexts. We’ll specify exactly where and retention duration.

[22:59] Tanya Brooks: Fine.

[23:01] Samir Patel: Another technical question: do you support “no data at rest” in hosted? Like, nothing stored.

[23:07] Markus Klein: There is always some operational metadata. If you mean “no payload stored,” yes as discussed. If you mean literally zero logs, that’s not realistic for a managed service. That’s one reason Private exists.

[23:21] Samir Patel: Makes sense.

[23:23] Laura Gomez: Can we ask about audit log access—who can see our logs on your side.

[23:28] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Limited to authorized personnel with business need, and access is logged. We can provide our access policy summary.

[23:38] Priya Nair: Do you have ISO 27001.

[23:41] Olga Petrov: Not currently certified. SOC 2 is our primary external assurance. We can discuss roadmap, but we won’t promise dates.

[23:52] Tanya Brooks: Okay.

[23:54] Eli Chen: About compliance: any HITRUST.

[23:57] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Not at this time.

[24:00] Tanya Brooks: That’s fine if SOC 2 is strong and the architecture keeps PHI out.

[24:06] Markus Klein: For the pilot, we can also discuss data minimization—tokenization/redaction before sending prompts—if you want an extra layer.

[24:15] Samir Patel: We have a redaction service already.

[24:18] Markus Klein: Great.

[24:20] Priya Nair: Audit logs again: do they include model changes—like if you swap a model version.

[24:26] Marcus Lin: Yes, model deployment changes are auditable. In Dedicated/Private you can pin model versions and control rollouts. Those actions are recorded.

[24:39] Tanya Brooks: Good.

[24:41] Avery Johnson: I’m going to pause and do a quick recap to ensure we’re aligned.

[24:45] Avery Johnson: So: you’re evaluating Dedicated as a near-term option but likely Private in VPC. Key requirements are: no prompt/output retention (or ability to disable), exportable audit logs to SIEM for 1 year, residency pinned to US, strong access controls with SSO/RBAC, and standard security evidence (SOC2 Type II, pen test summary, subprocessors, IR/DR summaries). Anything missing.

[25:09] Tanya Brooks: Add: explicit statement about not training on our data.

[25:13] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[25:14] Laura Gomez: And DPA/BAA conversation.

[25:17] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[25:18] Samir Patel: And a follow-up technical session on VPC connectivity and log export.

[25:23] Avery Johnson: Great.

[25:25] Priya Nair: I also need to know if you have a customer portal for compliance docs. Like a trust center.

[25:30] Olga Petrov: We have a trust center with high-level docs. The detailed reports are shared under NDA through secure channels. 

[25:40] Priya Nair: Okay.

[25:42] Tanya Brooks: Let’s talk about audit log categories again, because that’s where vendors hide stuff. Do you log query content in audit logs.

[25:50] Marcus Lin: Audit logs are for administrative and security-relevant events, not query content. Query content would only be in application logs if content logging is enabled, which we can disable.

[26:04] Tanya Brooks: Good.

[26:06] Eli Chen: Can you support sending logs to Splunk HEC.

[26:10] Markus Klein: Yes, via HTTPS endpoint. We’ll verify what we support as “native” and what requires a forwarder.

[26:18] Eli Chen: Ok.

[26:20] Samir Patel: Performance isn’t the topic today but we’ll ask later. 

[26:23] Avery Johnson: We can do that in the next session.

[26:26] Priya Nair: Can you confirm you do background checks on employees.

[26:30] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes, for relevant roles, including those with production access. We can provide a policy statement.

[26:39] Priya Nair: Ok. Security training.

[26:41] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Annual plus onboarding, with phishing simulations.

[26:47] Priya Nair: Great.

[26:49] Laura Gomez: Data breach history.

[26:52] Dr. Aisha Rahman: No material breaches to disclose. If you need formal language, we can provide it.

[27:00] Tanya Brooks: Good.

[27:02] Eli Chen: For Private, do you support running in our Kubernetes, or is it a managed thing.
